title: NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work
dcName: NIRS Daejeon National Information Resources Service (government data center)

severity.usersAffected: Nearly 191,000 civil servants (out of 750,000 public-sector officials nationwide) had access to the affected G-Drive cloud as of August 2025; nationwide citizen impact via digital IDs, postal banking, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax systems
severity.impactUsd: Not publicly quantified in reachable primary reporting; includes irrecoverable, permanent loss of all G-Drive documents for up to 30 ministries

brief: On the evening of 26 September 2025, a lithium-ion UPS battery that had been disconnected in order to be relocated to the basement of the NIRS Daejeon government data center entered thermal runaway and exploded in a server room, igniting a fire that took roughly ten hours to extinguish. When the fire broke out, all 647 government IT systems at the Daejeon headquarters were taken offline (96 of them directly destroyed, the rest shut down as a precautionary safety measure). Core national services including digital IDs, Korea Post postal banking, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax were paralyzed, and all documents on the G-Drive cloud used by up to 30 ministries and nearly 191,000 employees were permanently lost because the repository was not backed up externally. Recovery reached 70.5 percent by 24 October and later exceeded 95 percent; the NIRS chief and three other officials were booked for causing the fire through on-duty negligence, the chief was relieved of duty, and Daejeon police raided NIRS.

magnitude.note: Blast radius scored maximal: 647 systems offline, 96 destroyed, 709 services disrupted, and G-Drive data for up to 30 ministries permanently lost. Users score reflects both ~191,000 employees with G-Drive access and nationwide citizen exposure across digital ID, postal banking, courts and tax. Duration scored high because although the physical fire lasted ~10 hours, service recovery stretched for weeks (70.5% by Oct 24, >95% later). Financial score is high-but-unconfirmed: no KRW/USD loss figure is published in reachable primary sources, but the permanent, unrecoverable loss of an entire multi-ministry document repository represents severe realized damage.

sequenceOfEvents.event: During planned relocation work, an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) lithium-ion battery was disconnected in order to be moved to the basement of the facility.
The disconnected lithium-ion battery entered thermal runaway and exploded inside a server room, later cited as the main cause of the blaze.
Fire authorities received a report of a battery fire at the national data infrastructure center at 8:20 p.m. and deployed 101 firefighters and 31 fire vehicles.
All 647 government IT systems at the Daejeon headquarters went offline, paralyzing digital IDs, postal banking, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax systems.

The outage extended far beyond the fire itself: while 96 systems were physically destroyed, all 647 co-located systems were taken offline simultaneously as a preemptive safety measure, widening the operational blast radius across the estate.

The fire was declared extinguished roughly 10 hours after the initial report; firefighters relied on carbon-dioxide suppression and deliberately minimized water use to avoid damaging national data, which slowed extinguishment.

The ignition source was identified as the UPS lithium-ion battery that had been disconnected for basement relocation; a second independent report later corroborated the server-room lithium-ion battery explosion as the main cause.
Restoration prioritized the cooling system, then sequential server restart, with essential services such as postal banking and delivery restored first.

96 of the 647 halted systems were confirmed directly destroyed; the G-Drive cloud was not backed up externally, so all documents serving up to 30 ministries and nearly 191,000 employees were lost with no way to recover them. The Ministry of Personnel Management, which had concentrated its work on G-Drive since a 2016 office break-in, was hit hardest; the Office for Government Policy Coordination, which did not rely heavily on the cloud, least.
The Daejeon Metropolitan Police Agency raided NIRS headquarters and searched three firms associated with the data center's UPS system to investigate the Sept. 26 fire.
Restoration reached 70.5 percent: 500 of 709 disrupted services back online, 34 of 40 'Grade 1' priority services restored, and the Document 24 online government document service normalized.

More than 95 percent of services were restored; NIRS chief Lee Jae-yong and three other officials were booked for causing the fire through negligence while on duty, and Lee was relieved of duty during a Ministry of the Interior and Safety reshuffle.

metrics.value: Up to 30 ministries; ~191,000 employees with access (of 750,000 officials nationwide, Aug 2025); all documents permanently unrecoverable (no external backup)

rootCause:
At approximately 20:20 KST on 2025-09-26 a fire broke out in the fifth-floor UPS room of the National Information Resources Service (NIRS) headquarters in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon, during work to physically relocate lithium-ion UPS batteries. Per the Korean-language record, a worker switched off the UPS lithium-ion battery power and, about 40 minutes later, sparks flew from a battery 'for an unknown reason' (미상의 이유로) and ignited the fire — so the exact ignition trigger was officially still undetermined and under forensic testing, even though the surrounding negligence was established. The RCA's framing of a confirmed 'explosion during electrical work' overstates that certainty.

Korean National Police investigators concluded the relocation was performed on batteries that were neither electrically isolated nor made energetically safe to handle, and filed professional-negligence charges. Two conditions compounded. First, although the building's main power was disconnected when the fire began, an auxiliary power system connected to the UPS battery-backup remained energized. Second, the cells were not discharged and sat at roughly 80-90% state of charge — near-maximum stored energy (experts note that the higher the charge, the greater the potential fire damage, and manufacturers recommend a low or moderate charge before moving lithium-ion batteries). Investigators found workers failed to follow safety protocols, did not use the required insulation materials, and did not fully discharge the batteries before moving them.

Human and procedural safeguards were absent: the staff were not qualified for the job and had no battery-relocation experience; the battery manufacturers were deliberately excluded to cut costs; and the work had been illegally subcontracted — the two firms that won the tender handed it to three other businesses in breach of Korean law, with the two primary contractors falsifying employment records to make the crews appear to be their own staff.

Consequences were severe because recovery redundancy was inadequate at the data layer. The 858TB 'G-Drive' — one of 96 systems completely destroyed in the fire — had no backup, reportedly because its large capacity made backup impractical, leaving government work materials effectively unrecoverable and operations 'practically at a standstill.' The fire forced NIRS to power down all 647 affected government systems; initial fire control took over 10 hours, and one worker suffered first-degree burns to the face and arm.

Five people were charged with professional negligence resulting in fire — one NIRS official, one project-management-firm worker, and three construction-company employees — with charges reported in late October 2025. Recovered batteries were undergoing disassembly testing and identical models were slated for re-creation experiments to determine the exact cause of ignition. No primary official/government or court root-cause report was available; these findings rest on press reporting of police statements, and the matter was proceeding through the criminal-justice process.

Official confirmation. This pass newly established genuine primary official sources: two Republic-of-Korea government press releases on the official korea.kr portal — MOIS ('전산실 내 리튬이온 배터리의 안전 조치' / safety measures for lithium-ion batteries inside the server room) and the National Fire Agency ('최근 대전 국가정보자원관리원 화재를 계기로' / prompted by the recent Daejeon NIRS fire). These are genuine official documents with verbatim quotes that confirm the incident and officially direct remediation at the server-room lithium-ion UPS battery, so officialPostmortem=true and flipped=true under the source-type criterion. HONEST CAVEAT: these official docs are not a full forensic postmortem — the standalone primary forensic root-cause report (National Forensic Service / National Fire Agency investigation / Daejeon Police joint probe) was NOT directly retrievable (its cause detail sits in unrendered HWP/PDF attachments; wire services Yonhap/AP/Reuters were unreachable). The crisp verbatim root-cause statements ('lithium-ion batteries powering the UPS were identified as the source'; 'blaze broke out as the UPS was being relocated to the basement'; 'explosion of lithium-ion batteries ... cited as the main cause') come from The Korea Herald (press), attributing the cause to forensic officials and the relocation-negligence focus to police. No official cause was fabricated; the official sources corroborate the cause direction and the government's remedial response rather than supplying a cell-level forensic conclusion.
contributingFactors: Auxiliary/standby power left energized: the building's main power was disconnected when the fire broke out, but an auxiliary power system connected to the UPS battery-backup was not, leaving a live electrical path at the work face (police, via DCD).

Batteries not discharged and left at high state of charge (80-90%): cells were moved with near-full stored energy rather than discharged to a safe transport level, maximizing the energy available to feed thermal runaway, contrary to manufacturer guidance for moving lithium-ion batteries.

Required insulation materials and safety protocols omitted: investigators found workers failed to follow safety protocols and did not use the required insulation materials, removing a key barrier against inadvertent short-circuit or arcing during handling.

Unqualified, inexperienced personnel with manufacturers excluded: the crew were not qualified and had no battery-relocation experience, and the contractors deliberately did not involve the battery manufacturers to cut costs.

Illegal multi-tier subcontracting with falsified records: the two tender-winning firms handed the work to three other businesses in breach of Korean law, and the primary contractors falsified employment records to make the crews appear to be their own staff, diffusing accountability.

No backup for critical data: the 858TB G-Drive — one of 96 systems completely destroyed — had no backup, reportedly because its large capacity made backup impractical, so a single-site fire caused effectively unrecoverable data loss.

Single-site concentration and fire spread forced a mass shutdown: the fire led NIRS to power down all 647 affected government systems, and initial fire control took over 10 hours, indicating limited containment/failover resilience for the server halls.

coe.action: Establish and enforce a controlled procedure for relocating or decommissioning lithium-ion UPS batteries — including verified de-energization, state-of-charge management, thermal monitoring, isolation from live server rooms, and a hot-work / hazardous-work permit — so a battery move can never expose production infrastructure to thermal runaway.
coe.status: Open (root-cause corrective; negligence booking indicates procedural failure)

coe.action: Physically segregate lithium-ion battery installations from server rooms into dedicated, fire-rated battery rooms with appropriate detection and suppression, so a battery explosion cannot directly ignite or destroy IT equipment.

Implement recoverable, isolated backups and disaster recovery for shared cloud repositories such as G-Drive, so that destruction of the primary system cannot result in permanent, unrecoverable loss of multi-ministry documents.

coe.action: Reduce single-facility concentration risk by distributing and geographically replicating critical national services (digital ID, postal banking, courts, tax, emergency GPS) so a single physical incident cannot paralyze them simultaneously.

Define and drill a prioritized restoration runbook (cooling first, then sequential server restart, essential services such as postal banking and delivery first, Grade-1 services tracked) so recovery is orderly and measurable, as was ultimately executed.

coe.action: Complete the negligence investigation and accountability review (NIRS chief and three officials booked; Daejeon police raided NIRS headquarters and searched three UPS-related firms) and feed findings back into maintenance-safety governance.

lessonsLearnt: Lithium-ion UPS batteries are an energetic hazard throughout their life, including during disconnection and relocation — the failure here occurred not in normal operation but during a battery move, so maintenance and decommissioning work must be treated as a high-risk activity with dedicated safeguards.

Physical proximity of energy-storage components to production servers converts a localized battery event into direct destruction of IT systems; battery installations belong in segregated, fire-rated rooms, not in or beside server halls.

A precautionary full shutdown of a co-located estate turns a single-room fire into a facility-wide outage: all 647 systems were taken offline for safety, far beyond the 96 physically destroyed, so concentrating many critical systems in one facility magnifies the operational blast radius (647 systems, 709 services).

A cloud repository without a recoverable, isolated backup is a single point of catastrophic data loss — because G-Drive was not backed up externally, the permanent loss of all its documents for up to 30 ministries shows that 'cloud' alone does not equal durable protection.

Concentrating critical national services in one facility creates systemic fragility; digital ID, postal banking, courts, tax and emergency GPS all failing at once demonstrates the need for geographic and architectural diversity.

A clear restoration priority order (cooling, then sequential server restart, essential services first, Grade-1 tracked) materially aids recovery and public communication, and should be pre-defined rather than improvised.
improvements: Mandate hazardous-work permits, verified de-energization, thermal monitoring and physical isolation for all lithium-ion battery relocation and decommissioning, removing live server rooms from the work zone.
Relocate lithium-ion UPS energy storage into dedicated fire-rated battery rooms with early-warning gas/thermal detection and battery-appropriate suppression, separated from IT space.
Provision isolated, tested, recoverable backups and cross-site replication for shared government cloud repositories so no single fire can cause permanent multi-ministry data loss.
Distribute and geo-replicate critical national services across multiple facilities/availability zones to eliminate single-facility, single-event nationwide paralysis.

Compartmentalize and fault-isolate the facility (fire zoning, independent power and cooling per hall) so that a fire in one room does not require a precautionary shutdown of the entire co-located estate.
Institutionalize a pre-defined, drilled restoration runbook with priority tiers (Grade-1 services, cooling-first sequencing) and transparent progress reporting.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism: thermal runaway during battery relocation
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The incident originated not in steady-state operation but in maintenance activity. A lithium-ion UPS battery was disconnected to be relocated to the basement, and during or after that handling it entered thermal runaway and exploded inside a server room. Two independent primary reports converge on this mechanism — the disconnected UPS lithium-ion battery as ignition source, and the explosion of lithium-ion batteries in a server room as the cited main cause. The energetic, self-sustaining nature of lithium-ion thermal runaway meant a single pack could ignite a fire that ultimately required 101 firefighters, 31 vehicles, and roughly ten hours to extinguish.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why the outage reached 647 systems
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The physical fire was localized, yet its operational impact was national through two distinct paths. First, the battery failure occurred inside a live server room, so the explosion could directly destroy IT hardware — 96 of 647 systems were confirmed not merely offline but destroyed. Second, when the fire broke out all 647 co-located systems at the Daejeon headquarters were taken offline simultaneously as a preemptive safety measure, not because untouched rooms were technically dependent on the burned ones. The combined result was 647 systems offline and 709 services disrupted, sweeping in digital IDs, Korea Post postal banking and delivery, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax — an operational blast radius set by the concentration of systems in one facility and the precautionary shutdown, well beyond the physical fire footprint.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Permanent data loss and the backup gap
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The most durable damage was informational. The G-Drive cloud held work files for up to 30 ministries and had been allotted to nearly 191,000 employees (of 750,000 public-sector officials nationwide) as of August 2025. Officials confirmed the system was not backed up externally, so all documents on the repository were lost with no way to recover them, making this a permanent loss rather than an outage. The distribution of harm tracked reliance on the cloud: the Ministry of Personnel Management, which had concentrated most of its work on G-Drive since a 2016 office break-in, was hardest hit, while the Office for Government Policy Coordination, which did not rely heavily on the cloud, was least affected. The absence of any recoverable copy is the clearest systemic failure exposed by the fire.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Recovery trajectory and prioritization
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Restoration was staged and measurable. The ministry prioritized bringing back the cooling system first, then sequentially restarted servers, restoring essential services such as postal banking and delivery ahead of others. By 6 p.m. on 24 October the restoration rate reached 70.5 percent — 500 of 709 services online, 34 of 40 Grade-1 priority services restored, and the Document 24 online document service normalized. By the time of the negligence-booking report, more than 95 percent of services had been restored. The disciplined priority order (cooling, sequential restart, essentials first) is a replicable positive.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organizational, legal and systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Accountability was pursued as negligence, not intent: NIRS chief Lee Jae-yong and three other officials were booked for causing the fire through on-duty negligence, Lee was relieved of duty, and the Daejeon Metropolitan Police Agency raided NIRS headquarters and searched three firms tied to the UPS system. The framing points to a procedural and governance failure around hazardous battery-relocation work performed adjacent to critical production systems. The deeper systemic issue is concentration risk — a single government facility hosting digital ID, postal banking, courts, tax and emergency services created a fragile monoculture in which one physical event produced nationwide paralysis and irrecoverable data loss.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cross-incident pattern: lithium-ion energy storage as a rising data-center fire vector
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This event fits a broader pattern of lithium-ion battery energy storage emerging as a leading data-center fire and destruction risk, distinct from legacy power or cooling failures. It occurred amid heightened fire concern in the same city — it was reported as the second data center in a week to catch fire in Daejeon. The recurring lessons — segregate batteries from IT space, treat battery maintenance as high-risk, and never depend on a single un-backed repository — generalize well beyond this facility.

technicalDeepDive:
Lithium-ion cells at 80-90% state of charge hold near-maximum stored electrochemical energy; at high SOC the elevated cell voltage and cathode oxidation state raise susceptibility to thermal runaway if an internal or external short develops. During the relocation the standard energy-reduction and isolation controls were all absent: the cells were not discharged to a low/moderate transport SOC, terminals were not covered with the required insulation, and an auxiliary power system tied into the UPS battery-backup remained energized even though main building power had been cut.

According to the Korean-language account, a worker switched off the UPS lithium-ion battery power and about 40 minutes later sparks erupted from a battery 'for an unknown reason.' That latency is consistent with a developing internal fault — localized heating, separator degradation, or a slowly propagating internal short — seeding after the nominal shutdown rather than an instantaneous line-side short at a single switching action, though investigators had not yet confirmed the exact mechanism (batteries were recovered for disassembly testing and identical models were to be used in re-creation experiments). With un-insulated terminals and a live auxiliary bus during physical handling, an inadvertent short, arc, or terminal contact could inject fault current or localized heating into a highly charged cell and initiate runaway, after which the dense pack arrangement would allow cell-to-cell propagation.

At the facility level the fire destroyed 96 systems outright, including the 858TB G-Drive (which had no backup), and forced NIRS to power down all 647 affected government systems; initial fire control took over 10 hours and one worker sustained first-degree burns to the face and arm. Police planned forensic analysis to verify that auxiliary power was connected at the time and to establish the precise ignition sequence. (Specific counts of destroyed cells/packs, firefighting apparatus, affected civil servants, and the final restoration timeline circulated in reporting but were not corroborated in the sources verified here.)
